88ca090372f0c832534d0187a3e8ed2f.text: An attempted break-in reported on early Monday morning at Delainey's Lock & Key, a store in downtown Williams Lake. The business's security camera captured the face of one of the man trying to break in. An attempted break-in was reported early Monday morning at Delainey’s Lock & Key in Williams Lake. The incident has left Krista Storoschuk, owner of Delainey’s, facing damage to her business and renewed frustration, about 11 months after two thieves broke in and stole approximately $5,000 worth of hunting knives. Storoschuk said her security cameras recorded someone trying to force open the business’s door at approximately 5:03 a.m. on Oct. 26. Storoschuk said the footage showed someone repeatedly shouldering and kicking the door before using a hammer to pry off part of the frame. The door sustained damage, but the lock held and no one gained entry. She added that one person tilted a security camera, apparently trying to avoid being recorded, but the movement instead provided a close view of the person’s face. “No one was on the property at the time,” Storoschuk said. Although the building has an alarm, it did not activate because no one entered. After waking and reviewing the camera alerts, Storoschuk contacted RCMP at approximately 8 a.m. She said an officer attended and she provided surveillance videos and a close-up image of the person’s face. According to Storoschuk, the officer planned to consult colleagues to see whether anyone recognized the people recorded and said police will follow up with her. The incident comes approximately 11 months after a previous break-in at the business. Storoschuk said two people smashed the glass in the main entrance and entered the store. She shared, “They did gain entry to my establishment and stole about $5,000 worth of hunting knives.” She also said the police examined the scene for identifying evidence. Interior security cameras recorded the intruders, but their faces were covered. “We never found the culprits,” she added

c50bfbd6018fd15937ce3be3108dacbf.text: Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA-elect Lorne Doerkson (l) speaks with a resident in Cache Creek while on the campaign trail on Oct. 4. Doerkson led the BC Conservatives to a resounding victory on Oct. 24, and is on track to become the province's next premier, and the first from the Interior since 1986. British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Of the last five B.C. premiers, three were political staffers and two were lawyers, and many MLAs start their road to the provincial legislature via local politics: the MLAs-elect for the two Kamloops ridings bordering Cariboo-Chilcotin, Peter Milobar and Ward Stamer, were first the mayors of Kamloops and Barriere respectively. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. He previously sold advertising for the Salmon Arm Observer and worked as publisher for three other papers owned by David Black’s Black Press Media: the now-defunct Prince George Free Press, as well as the Williams Lake Tribune and 100 Mile Free

As the dust settles on the 2026 snap B.C. election, the Conservative Party is poised to take two-thirds of the legislative seats, and the NDP is looking for a new leader. Ravi Parmar, who eked out a third victory for the NDP in Langford-Highlands, says voters “sent a message” that the snap election was the “wrong decision.” “It was clearly a mistake. No question,” Parmar said in a Monday morning interview. “We spent the entire election campaign answering the question, ‘ Why did we call an election?’ And I think that became a huge detriment to us and a huge detriment to our leader.” Outgoing premier David Eby called the election two years early, presumably banking on internal Conservative Party division to carry his party to an easy victory, and justifying the call by saying he needed a new mandate to take on U.S. trade threats. University of British Columbia political science lecturer Stewart Prest says this may go down in history as the biggest snap election blunder in Canadian history, calling it a complete “own goal” by the B.C. NDP. Prest says Eby compounded his mistakes by running a “tone-deaf” and negative campaign, seeking partisan advantage “by hook or by crook.” “It really does speak to a government caught up in its own hubris,” Prest said, “caught up in the partisanship of it all.” One of this election’s key storylines is record-low turnout. Slightly more than 48 per cent of British Columbians voted. Totals were down for both the Conservatives and NDP compared to 2024, with the Conservative Party recording about 50,000 fewer votes and the NDP down about 275,000, according to preliminary counts. Mario Canseco of the polling firm Research Co. says several factors could be at play, including the rainy weather. 6a88f06c92546a6825cf1e589c4b7f31.text: Fake campaign signs pop up in B.C. riding on election eve | Williams Lake Tribune Fraudulent (left) and legitimate Green Party sign (right) for candidate Tim Binnema in the Surrey-Fleetwood riding. Who would bother to make and put up fake election campaign signs without a candidate’s consent? Green Party candidate in Surrey-Fleetwood, Binnema says someone put up hundreds of unauthorized signs with his name and photo last Friday (Oct. 23), a day before final voting in the B.C. election. “It’s somewhere between 100 and 200 (signs), I would say,” Binnema estimated Saturday. “It was shocking, to tell you the truth. When I turned around the corner and saw my mug (on signs), I thought, ‘Oh my goodness, how did this happen?'” The fake campaign signs feature a photo of Binnema, unlike his legitimate signs. His photo is “obviously ripped from the website,” and the signs have the wrong shade of green, he noted. “The signs say that they were authorized by my financial agent, which obviously wasn’t the case,” added Binnema, who works for an engineering company as a manager. “If you drive down 152nd (Street) near 96th (Avenue), you will notice an interesting pattern which might suggest how those signs got there,” he wrote in an email to *Surrey* *Now-Leader*. Later Saturday, Binnema clarified the situation in a phone call. “There were a whole bunch of signs that got put up last night all around Surrey and Fleetwood, including a bunch of, ‘Why a snap election? and some ‘Vote NDP out’ (signs),” Binnema said from his home in Fleetwood. “Some of my fraudulent signs were located next to those signs, so you can draw your conclusions who might have done that.” It wouldn’t take a conspiracy theorist to suggest the signs were an attempt to split the vote in Surrey-Fleetwood, where Conservative candidate Garry Purewal won with 8,691 votes over NDP incumbent Jagrup Brar (6,522 votes), followed by Binnema in third with 1,030, at last count. a2c8500e39b2dff4f6c618298aabffff.text: B.C. North Coast LNG project draws nearer to final investment decision | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. North Coast LNG project draws nearer to final investment decision Stephen Del Regno, Western LNG (left) at a signing ceremony for the Heads of Agreement with SEFE in May 2026. SEFE has now converted that preliminary deal into a 20-year commitment to buy one million tonnes of LNG per year. A floating LNG liquefaction facility proposed for north of Prince Rupert has now secured binding contracts for more than half its planned production. On Oct. 26, Ksi Lisims LNG announced it had converted its May 2026 heads of agreement to a binding sale and purchase agreement (SPA) with Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE), a state-owned German energy company. Under the agreement, SEFE would purchase one million tonnes of LNG per annum (mtpa) over 20 years. This brings Ksi Lisims completed binding SFAs to 7 million mtpa, or roughly 58 per cent, of the 12 million mtpa the company plans to produce once in production currently scheduled to begin in the early 2030s. It also brings the Western LNG, Rockies LNG and Nisga’a Nation partnership closer to the goal of having a final investment decision (FID) by the end of 2026. Large scale energy projects typically need at least 75 per cent of their project capacity locked into long-term deals to secure bank and institutional financing. A spokesperson for Western LNG said the company expects to have such deals signed for all 12 mtpa and an FID this year. “The project remains on track to reach full commercialization by the end of the year,” a press release stated. “Each new agreement brings Ksi Lisims LNG closer to construction, and closer to the jobs, training and long-term revenue our people have worked toward for generations,” said Eva Clayton, president of the Nisga’a Lisims Government. “As a co-developer, our Nation is proving that Canada’s resources can reach world markets in a way that respects our lands and our rights. f06871d0f3f062d436c0523ffe11e5c9.text: B.C. election outcome does not reflect popular vote | Williams Lake Tribune The graph on the left shows the seats in the legislature following the Oct. 24 British Columbia provincial election. However, the voter support, seen in the graph on the right, tells a different story of the wishes of the voters. The British Columbia provincial election on Oct. 24 gave the Conservatives a majority government, winning 64 of 93 seats in the legislature, with the New Democratic Party winning 27 seats and the BC Greens winning two. However, the voter statistics told a different story: fewer than half of voters marked their ballots for a Conservative. A total of 48.1 per cent of voters cast ballots for the Conservatives, while 37.4 per cent voted for a BC NDP candidate and 11 per cent supported a BC Green candidate. The remaining 3.5 per cent of voters supported all other parties, including OneBC and Centre BC. OneBC received support from 1.5 per cent of voters, and Centre BC had support from 1.6 per cent of voters. Under the first-past-the-post election structure in British Columbia and at the federal level, it is possible for a party to win a majority of seats despite having lower support from the voters. Fair Vote Canada has criticized the voting structure and is calling for a proportional representation system, similar to the electoral systems used in more than 80 per cent of western democracies. “In many countries with proportional representation, cooperation across the aisle is the norm and better long-term outcomes on the economy, health and the environment are the result,” the organization said in a statement. “For the sake of all BC voters, it’s time to put proportional representation back on the agenda.” Fair Vote Canada said a 2025 poll showed that 75 per cent of British Columbians would support a proportional representation system. Residents of the Fairview encampment in Penticton have until Friday, Oct. 30 at 12 p.m. to leave or they will be evicted after a court order issued on Oct. 26. Around two years after it was established, the encampment of unhoused individuals off Highway 97 in Penticton has been ordered to be cleared by a B.C. Justice. In her oral reasons for judgement, Justice Briana Hardwick issued an injunction barring the occupation of the road dedication that had been transformed into an impromptu fenced community of tents and temporary structures, with it coming into effect at noon on Oct. 30. The injunction requires all of the temporary structures to be cleared, and all of the residents of the encampment to vacate the area. Over more than an hour in Penticton Supreme Court, and ahead of longer written reasons that will be published later in the week, Justice Hardwick gave a shortened breakdown of her findings, in particular that ordering a single specific property to be cleared did not violate any of the residents’ rights, and that by forcing them to leave it would not increase the risks they already face as unhoused individuals. “Neither the general evidence of the social problems of homelessness, or the defendants’ sincere subjective views on the Fairview Encampments benefits demonstrate the requisite causal connection required to establish a breach of Section 7 of the Charter,” Hardwick said. “In summary, I find that the Fairview Encampment presents a significant ongoing public safety risk, the road dedication is simply unsuitable in any condition for an encampment.” Justice Hardwick noted that the ongoing risk of fires presented by the encampment were well

1292bf8ecdaafbec004ceaf3d29054ab.text: Two ferry sailings are at risk early Thursday amid Georgia Strait wind warning. BC Ferries’ CEO Nicolas Jimenez has moved on for unspecified reasons, and BC Ferries’ board says it initiated a leadership transition and launched a revitalization review. According to BC Ferries, Brian Anderson, vice president of strategy and planning, has been appointed as the interim CEO, while Dallyn Willis, executive vice president and chief financial officer, assumes responsibility for strategy and planning and leads the revitalization review with oversight from the board. “The ferry system is a lifeline for coastal residents and businesses, and critical to the province’s economy. The review will define new ways to optimize the system and improve how BC Ferries delivers services for customers and coastal communities,” noted a news release from BC Ferries. Under the Coastal Ferry Act, BC Ferries undergoes a regulatory review and contract discussions every four years to set limits on fares and establish required service levels. “The board thanks outgoing CEO Nicolas Jimenez for his contributions to BC Ferries and wishes him success in his future endeavours,” noted the release. Jimenez was appointed as CEO in March 2023. Over his tenure, he has overseen price hikes and the controversial plan for a Chinese company to build four new major hybrid-electric vessels by spring 2029. Over the provincial election, the BC NDP was under fire from the Conservatives for overloaded routes, cancelled sailings and high fares. The new majority Conservative government has floated the idea of a B.C. Ferries Charter, which would set standards for reliability, on-time performance, capacity, affordability and customer service. BC Ferries says a formal search for a permanent successor to Jimenez will follow the review.

1c293bae0bddba8d3da1d6d814cc960d.text: BC NDP candidate Stephanie Higginson has pulled ahead in the Ladysmith-Oceanside riding, after preliminary results of the provincial election were corrected. Higginson now sits at 13,380 (44.37 per cent), 13 votes ahead of Kris McNichol of the BC Conservative Party’s 13,367 votes (44.33 per cent). Charlene Smylie of the BC Green Party sits in third place with 3,365 votes (11.16 per cent). Elections BC noted Monday that results reported on election night are preliminary and subject to change as they are verified for accuracy and completeness. The results were updated last night (Oct. 25) to correct a data entry error, according to Elections BC. “A recount of the results reported on election night will take place for Ladysmith-Oceanside,” Elections BC said in an email. “There are also absentee and mail-in ballots left to count in that district.” The recount and count of absentee and mail-in ballots will take place from Nov. 6 to Nov. 10. Results will not be finalized until these counts are complete. “I think there’s still a lot of unknowns,” Higginson said. “It’s always nice to be going into a recount on the higher side of the ledger, but we have learned in this election not to take anything for granted.” Higginson added her priorities, if elected, will be to check-in with the new mayors and councils and First Nations and see what their priorities are. Preliminary election night results from Oct. 24 previously had McNichol ahead by 89 votes. McNichol said there will be a recount and every vote will be counted and noted the change was due to “a human error”. “This is democracy at its finest,” he added. “We’ll see what happens in the recount and the mail-in ballots and all those ballots.” If elected, McNichol said his first priority is to see the new cath lab built at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital.

f5eba8432acb12d1cc1b181ed2fcbd28.text: Halloween is a fun time for most people, but it can be a scary (and dangerous) time for pets and wildlife. Halloween is a fun time for many people, but it can present plenty of hazards for animals, both domestic and wild. Loud noises such as doorbells ringing, unexpected visitors and open doors, fireworks, exposure to potential toxins, and discarded candy wrappers are all things that can make animals anxious or present health threats. Here are three important tips to keep pets safe: **1) Keep the candy away from your pets:** While pets can enjoy their own treats or small portions of plain pumpkin, many human candies can be toxic to dogs and cats. A study found that more than 40 per cent of chocolate toxicity-related claims in B.C. happen between October and December. Additionally, wrappers can be a choking hazard. If you suspect your pet has ingested toxic food or is choking, contact your vet. **2) Keep your pet’s environment calm:** Halloween fireworks and doorbells can be stressful, especially for senior or anxious pets. The BC SPCA reports a spike of emergency calls on Halloween night. It is best to create a safe, secure, and quiet area for your pets. Playing classical music in the background, or having a radio or TV on, helps cover outside noises, while familiar smells and items like a blanket can provide comfort. If your pet experiences extreme anxiety from fireworks, consult your vet in advance. **3) Update your pet’s ID registry:** It is best to keep pets safe and comfortable at home. However, with the door opening frequently for trick-or-treaters, pets can slip out and run away. Permanent identification (ID) like microchips or tattoos is essential for a safe return. However, IDs are only effective if they are registered and the information is up to date. Have you moved since registering your pet, or has your contact information changed? Students at Columneetza Junior Secondary School chose Surinderpal Rathor as the mayor of Williams Lake during the mock municipal elections as part of the CIVIX Student Vote program on Oct. 17. Total of 470 schools had submitted their Student Vote results for the 2026 local election, representing 94 municipalities and regional districts throughout B.C. Adults weren’t the only ones heading to the polls over the past two weeks, as Williams Lake students cast mock ballots in both provincial and municipal elections through CIVIX’s Student Vote program. Both local and provincial mock elections ran parallel with real elections in Williams Lake on Oct. 17 and Oct. 24. Four Williams Lake schools participated in the provincial Student Vote: Cataline Elementary, Mountview Elementary, Nesika Elementary and Sacred Heart Catholic School. If students in Williams Lake were deciding the outcome, the BC Greens would lead based on the average vote share across the four schools, with 38.74 per cent, followed by the BC Conservatives at 36.77 per cent and the BC NDP at 24.50 per cent. Williams Lake students were divided in their choices for MLA. At Cataline Elementary, BC Green Party candidate Douglas Gook led with 57.78 per cent of the vote, while Mountview Elementary students favoured BC Conservatives candidate Lorne Doerkson, who received 58.33 per cent of the vote. At Nesika Elementary, BC NDP candidate Kathryn Askee and BC Green Party candidate Douglas Gook tied with 40.91 per cent each. Doerkson also led at Sacred Heart Catholic School with 41.67 per cent. For municipal mock elections in Williams Lake, two schools actively participated in the mock municipal election, Columneetza Junior Secondary School with a 1351 voter turnout, and Nesika Elementary School with 83 voters. 300d8dd0b4ddd4cf617b01dae3680d79.text: Williams Lake Timberwolves celebrates their gold-medal win at the Nightmare on Ice tournament in Quesnel, where they defeated Smithers Storms 4-3 in overtime on Sunday, Oct 25. A Williams Lake Timberwolves players looks to scored against Quesnel Thunder during the Nightmare on Ice tournament. Williams Lake won the game 5-2. Williams Lake Timberwolves brought home gold with a 4-3 overtime victory over Smithers Storm at the Nightmare on Ice tournament in Quesnel on Sunday, Oct. 25. The tournament began Friday, Oct. 23, with the Timberwolves opening with an 8-1 win over Penticton Jr. Vees. Williams Lake suffered its only loss of the weekend on Saturday morning, falling 7-5 to the Smithers Storm. “Even though we didn’t win, I was really proud of how hard we fought back to make it a close game,” said Mike Bishop, coach of the Williams Lake Timberwolves. Some families stayed in Quesnel, while others travelled back to Williams Lake for Saturday’s 7 a.m. game against Smithers. Bishop said the early start made it difficult for players to get going. The Timberwolves rebounded in the afternoon with a 5-2 win over Quesnel, then advanced to the gold-medal game with an 8-2 semi-final win over Penticton on Sunday, setting up a rematch with Smithers. Williams Lake avenged Saturday’s loss with a 4-3 overtime victory over Smithers. Jaxon Benvin scored the winning goal at 4:04 of sudden-death overtime to secure gold. Bishop told the Tribune how demanding practices, Monday dryland training, and Wednesday spin classes and yoga helped players maintain their energy through a demanding schedule during the weekends. “As the tournament went along, our conditioning proved to be a benefit for the kids,” added Bishop. The physical demands were another challenge for some players experiencing full-contact hockey for the first time. 022534f2cae6a1c81c3ac41a80c51901.text: Artist Tiffany Jorgensen stands on scaffolding in front of her mural, which brings Chilcotin landscape to life in Williams Lake. The mural incorporates resident's memories of Chilcotin through wild horses, wildflowers and familiar landscapes. Tiffany Jorgensen has completed her section of the Cariboo Reflections mural, bringing the Chilcotin landscape to life outside a Williams Lake care home’s dining room. Jorgensen’s work is part of Cariboo Reflections, a collaborative mural on the Cariboo Regional District wall at 108 Third Avenue North. “We are doing a mural from morning to night for the residents of the care home here,” Jorgensen said. “Everybody picked a time of day, which was so funny because it came very organically.” Jorgensen’s section depicts the warm orange light of evening. Her section faces the care home’s dining room, where residents could watch the landscape take shape. Their comments and encouragement provided company while she painted, with one man giving her “the side eye and the thumbs up all the time,” she said. “I went in there and talked to everybody. Everybody is so excited,” Jorgensen said. Sarah Sigurdson, co-founder of Cariboo Art Beat, consulted residents about what they wanted to see. Residents suggested horses, wildflowers, mountains, ranching, logging and gold panning, along with details such as a particular red truck. The artists developed those suggestions into a connected design, Jorgensen explained. Some of the horses in Jorgensen’s newest mural carry more than a connection to the Cariboo landscape. They carry memories of animals that mattered to the people who knew them. Jorgensen asked about horses that had been special to care home residents and incorporated them into the mural, offering a way to honour those memories. She said the gesture drew appreciative responses from people who recognized the horses. a51f743c5fdb663ceebb10d058650a00.text: Former Finance minister Brenda Bailey is one of several NDP MLAs whose pension was vested on Oct. 23. By waiting until Oct. 24 to hold the B.C. snap provincial election, NDP Leader David Eby saved several of his party’s MLAs from losing their pensions. Had the election been called sooner — and there was plenty of pressure for Eby to do so as the Conservative Party floundered — several outgoing MLAs would have received no pension. Any member of the B.C. legislature first elected on Oct. 24, 2020, and re-elected in 2024 had their pensions vested on Oct. 23, 2026. NDP caucus communications director Edward May says that, from his understanding, pensions were not considered “at all” in timing the election call. “David Eby said the timing was because of the threat to British Columbian jobs and cost of living posed by U.S. tariffs, and the fact that B.C. NDP MLAs were being forced to vote from their hospital beds because one empty seat could have brought the government down,” May said via email. Nine NDP MLAs and three Conservative MLAs had their pensions secured the day before the election, including former Finance minister Brenda Bailey and former Emergency Management minister Kelly Greene, both of whom chose not to run for re-election, as well as Susie Chant and Harwinder Sandhu, both of whom lost. Also passing the threshold were Brittny Anderson, Jennifer Whiteside, Niki Sharma, Josie Osborne and Grace Lore from the NDP, and Lorne Doerkson, Bruce Banman and Trevor Halford from the Conservative Party, all of whom were re-elected. Current pension rules for B.C. legislators date back to 2007. Members of the legislature are entitled to a pension at an annual accrual rate of 3.5 per cent of their highest three-year average of pensionable earnings, capped at 70 per cent. All MLAs must contribute 11 per cent of earnings to the pension fund. MLAs with six years’ service will therefore receive a pension equal to 21 per cent of their top three-year average. 477b7eca0ca3ae9b32b13e9c799e5487.text: The B.C. NDP caucus is meeting this week to select an interim leader to replace David Eby. The B.C. NDP caucus is meeting this week to select an interim leader to replace David Eby, who announced he will step aside after leading his party to an ill-fated snap election. Both outgoing and new members of the legislature plan to meet. “Separately, the party will take a clear and honest look at the campaign and set the timing and process for a leadership race in the weeks and months ahead,” a caucus spokesperson said in an emailed statement. Outgoing Health minister Ravi Kahlon gave a few possible names for interim leader, including Mike Farnworth, who served as Eby’s NDP House leader; Josie Osborne, the outgoing Finance minister; Adrian Dix, a former party leader and outgoing Energy minister; and Niki Sharma, Eby’s attorney general. He also mentioned Ravi Parmar, Spencer Chandra Herbert or Jennifer Whiteside as possibilities. All served as ministers in Eby’s government. “There’s no shortage of very talented people,” said Kahlon, adding that he doesn’t expect the process to be divisive. Kahlon, who chose not to run for re-election, says he planned to focus on his family and wouldn’t consider serving as interim leader. “You never know what will happen in the future, but my focus medium-term is on my family,” he said. “Too early to say,” Parmar said. “I would say that I learned from my mentor in politics, \[former premier\] John Horgan, that before one should act, they should do a lot of listening and learning.” The NDP’s last leadership race was contentious. Eby ran against Anjali Appadurai, but was acclaimed after Appadurai was disqualified for allegedly breaking party electoral rules by working with outside organizations. University of British Columbia political science lecturer Stewart Prest says Eby never really found his stride after that leadership race. “I think it cast a pall over his leadership that he was never able to fully escape,” Prest said. 7b22d77e6c5e18e109b3d5ea75670ce0.text: After a tied vote, a judicial recount, and the drawing of lots, Jennifer Thoss has won election as mayor of the Village of Lytton. The Village of Lytton has a new mayor, after a judicial recount confirmed a tied vote for that position and the decision came down to the drawing of lots. Jennifer Thoss has been confirmed as the incoming mayor, after the recount and draw on Tuesday (Oct. 27). She and incumbent mayor Denise O’Connor each received 45 votes in the municipal election held on Oct. 17, and a recount produced the same outcome. According to CivicInfoBC, there were an estimated 198 eligible voters in Lytton in this election. “Ties are very rare, and only happen once in a blue moon,” said Shannon Story, chief election officer for the Village of Lytton. “But obviously when you’re dealing with a smaller municipality with smaller numbers, a tie is statistically more possible.” As per the Village of Lytton’s election procedure bylaw, and in accordance with the Local Government Act, the tie was referred to a judicial recount in Kamloops. When that recount confirmed the tie, the names of the two candidates were placed in a container, and one was drawn. a0a8ca22ee5d6268c687a2e87b672017.text: It came down to a draw, more than a week after the local government election, to determine the final seat in the Princeton town council election. The election was held on Oct. 17, but the vote resulted in a tie for the fourth of four councillor seats. On Oct. 26, Carrie Kassa, chief election officer for Princeton, declared Tyler Willis elected as councillor following a judicial recount lot draw. In the election, held on Oct. 14, Willis and Paula Shackleton were tied for the fourth spot on council, with each receiving 391 votes. Because of the tie, the decision was referred to a judicial recount. This involved recounting the ballots for the two councillors once more. Then, since the vote was still a tie, the winner was determined by a lot draw. This will be third term on council for Willis. He was elected in 2018 and 2022. The others on the Princeton town council are Spencer Coyne as mayor and Barb Gould, Doug Pateman and George Elliott as councillors. Coyne, Gould and Elliott were all members of the past council, while Pateman was a councillor from 2014 to 2018. In the Princeton election, 1,053 ballots were cast. There were an estimated 2,571 eligible voters. Gould finished 690 votes, followed by Pateman with 575 votes and Elliott with 501 votes. The remaining candidates were Amanda Werry with 375 votes, incumbent Randy McLean with 336 votes, Dayton Wales with 325 votes and Chris Obey with 290 votes. In 2008, Marilyn Harkness took the fourth seat on the council with 385 votes, just two more than fifth-place candidate Dina Slowikowski-Campbell. In 2011, Kim Maynard took the fourth spot with 465 votes, just 20 more than fifth-place candidate Ray Jarvis.

419b5d8d1d7c501bac9afa5a1011d810.text: Two ferry sailings are at risk early Thursday amid Georgia Strait wind warning. A dead humpback whale has been reported to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) near the site where a whale was struck by BC Ferries’ Queen of Surrey from Langdale to Horseshoe Bay terminals on Oct. 18. In an update on Tuesday, Oct. 27, the Marine Education and Research Society said the dead whale was sighted near the Grace Islands just over a week after reports of a ferry striking a whale in the same area. “Necropsy anticipated, but it is believed that external injuries indicate vessel strike,” noted the society. The society says passengers on the ferry saw the whale surface in front of the bow, travelling from right to left. “The whale then surfaced behind the ferry, thrashing, with red visible in the water. Passenger accounts indicate that the ferry did not slow after the collision and that there was no communication to passengers about the impact they felt or what follow-up actions might be taken,” the society said at the time. They said at the time that the strike was likely fatal due to the speed the vessel was travelling and how direct the hit is believed to have been, “however, a fatality may never be confirmed because dead whales often sink to the ocean floor.” In an emailed statement, BC Ferries said they are aware of reports that a deceased whale had been found in the area, and BC Ferries crews also spotted the whale and reported the sighting to Fisheries and Oceans Canada. “This is a very sad development, particularly following the collision involving the Queen of Surrey on Oct. 18. We recognize the concern this raises,” they noted. “At this point, we don’t know whether this is the same whale involved in the collision or what caused its death. We continue to cooperate fully with DFO and will provide whatever information we can to support their assessment.”
